utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner. A quick sprint to the end, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd like to finish with the cross-examination this morning with about 45 minutes to go, sir; and just discuss with the evacuation and take you through hospital and the evacuation, okay?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you are testified that you arrived at Vukovar Hospital on November 19th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you arrived there in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't stay there the whole evening or on a 24-hour basis, that you left sometime after midnight; midnight, 1.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After midnight, I went to the command post, my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while at the hospital on the 19th, you weren't given any orders to make a list of the persons in the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't given any such task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at no time did you attempt to identify the persons inside of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you really can't say for certain who those persons were that were in the hospital; you can't give us a list of names or identify all of those people there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you returned to the hospital on November 20th, correct, the following day?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you return to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this lapse of time, I can't remember what time it was, but it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified in Belgrade concerning the time that you arrived; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you testified a year and a half ago in Belgrade, was the information fresher in your mind?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information might have been fresher. But as I said yesterday, in the course of making all these statements and when certain documents were put to me or events, later on, I would link up one event with another. So that most probably, times and perhaps even dates do not always correspond in all the statements I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But since there were no documents relating to the evacuation on November 20th, which you're discussing, would you agree with me that your memory was fresher a year and a half ago when you testified in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, certainly, but I explained to you just now why my statements differ. If, when I made my first statement, certain facts had been put to me, my statement would certainly have been different. It doesn't mean that I gave a wrong statement, but my statement in that case would have been more correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the Belgrade transcripts which is 0461-9343 to 0461-9395, page 11, which is 0461-9349, to the bottom of the page. Thank you. Page 11 in the English, and it should be around the mid to the bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you see where it says,"Presiding judge: The following day -- in the morning, in the afternoon"?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Should be middle to the bottom, "Presiding judge: The following day."

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you could follow along with me I will read a portion of it "Presiding judge: The following day, in the morning -- in the afternoon." "Witness Radoje Paunovic: I cannot say exactly because I not there the whole time -- a while earlier, I said that as an officer, I wasn't there the whole time." "Presiding judge: Was Simic, as company commander, there?" "Witness Radoje Paunovic: Simic was there because the next day when I reinforced security -- as to the time when I got there, perhaps I got there around 1200 hours, at noon. I can't remember exactly." If you want to continue, you then say, . "The evacuation was carried out in the afternoon and this, well, let's call it a selection, even if I didn't know who got there or go there, and who would come here and since the buses were parked behind the hospital, my unit was not assigned to do the screening or whatever." Does that refresh your memory, sir? Did you get there around noon?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in my statement that I arrived around noon. But I'm telling you again, that not even when my -- I made my first statement or the second or the third or now, can I remember precisely what time it was. But I did attend the evacuation. I was there. When I referred to the afternoon and what I told you about yesterday, the taking out of the civilians and everything else, and I wasn't there all the time. If I said here at 12.00, I can't recall exactly what time it was. But I repeat, I was there during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at it to try and determine when you were there. Were you there when the security organs arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you there when they entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were already in, some were outside. I can't remember every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you -- could we turn to page 58 in the English, which is 0461-9372 of that same transcript. The top third of the page. Now, the question -- if we go to the top third of the page, start off with attorney Zaklan [phoen], "You let them inside and you were securing the hospital." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it be scrolled down a little bit. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "You let them inside and you were securing the hospital. You let them inside. How did you let them enter?" Then the presiding judge asked: "Was anyone in charge of the work of these men?" Then the attorney asks: "Was anyone in charge of the work of these security organs?" And the presiding judge asks you: "Do you know anything?" And you said: "I said I don't." How did you allow them inside? The presiding Judge said, "You just saw them when they were screening the people, so who told them to let them inside?" Answer: "Well certainly, I cannot remember the details and I wish to reiterate that I wasn't there non-stop, the whole 24 hours, so the commander or his deputy was there." "Q. Who was there and did you see who was there? Who was in command? I'm asking you whether you did or didn't, so please tell me whether you did or didn't?" "A. I didn't." Did you see these people enter? You indicated you don't know who let them inside.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What people do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These security people. You said you don't know who let them inside. Were you there when they arrived, and did you see them enter?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this statement in Belgrade, I said I didn't know who let them in. But what I'm telling you now is, there was no need for someone to let the chief of the security organ in. He had the right to go in. Secondly, when I say I was not inside, I was not in the hospital when the triage and screening and selection were being carried out. I was outside at that point. If I understand your question to be: Who let them in? No one had to let them in; they had the right to go in. They were not uninvited or uncalled for. And there is no doubt that they worked in the hospital; I mean, that they were doing their task in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, when asked by the court as to who let them inside, you didn't say that. You said, "I can't remember the details." You never said: They just walked in on their own. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not claiming even now that I remember the details. I'm just explaining that there's no need for anyone to let them inside, and that's what I said in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's try another factor. Were you present when Major Sljivancanin met with the hospital staff in the plaster room in the morning of November 20th?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, there were several different groups evacuated on that morning, and one of the groups were wounded persons. Were you present when the wounded persons were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when the wounded were evacuated, but they were not evacuated together with the healthy and the sick. They were separated off and transported in some kind of medical vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But were you -- you weren't present for that; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there at the beginning of this assignment, but then I left. I can't recall now why I had to leave, what other task I was performing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were not present for the evacuation of the wounded; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was there at the beginning, but I did not stay until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you testified in Belgrade, at page 48, that you were not present. So do you wish to change your testimony and say that you were present for the beginning and not the end or for the full time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I wasn't there until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that a evacuation operation is a complex matter.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also testified yesterday that due to the importance of this operation, an officer was placed on each bus.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your military police unit had several important functions during this evacuation, ranging from securing the hospital, securing the evacuee -- searching the evacuees, escorting the buses, providing security; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also had responsibilities in this evacuation for providing security to the buses, assigning persons, overseeing your soldiers or men.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as commander, you're responsible for your men; you have to watch them and give them assignments and make sure they act properly.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, as part of this evacuation, however, you never received any written order relating to this operation.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And to this day, you've never seen any written order; you claim you've never seen any written order.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yesterday and the day before yesterday, I said I did not exclude the possibility of such an order existing. But I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're claiming you don't know who was even in charge of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you've never seen a security assessment relating to the evacuation operation, any written security assessment.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you did not know what officers would be on the buses with your military policemen.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Nor did you know, according to your testimony, where your men were to escort the civilians were the hospital; where they would be going.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was probably the officers on the buses who knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, you don't even know what time you arrived, according to your testimony, at the hospital on that date.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when I arrived, but after this lapse of time, I certainly cannot remember exactly what time it was, but -- by the clock. But I am telling you that I was there during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that your claims or your testimony that you really didn't know what was happening during this evacuation are not true. That the importance of the evacuation and the important role you had, you would have had to have known who was in charge, who was responsible, and you would have had to have seen an order.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I knew or not, I carried out the task without any problems, and you can conclude whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After the cross-examination by the OTP, I will try to put some questions to you in order to clarify some issues. I think that you spoke a lot, and there are many of your evidences so let's go through them. Let us start from the final bit put to you by the Prosecution; namely, that you were not present at the evacuation when it was carried out, invoking your statement given before the Belgrade district court special war crimes department where you said that you came at around 12.00. You said yourself that you were not sure about time and that you even made mistakes about dates, which is quite understandable, given the passage of time. And then some documents were put to you to refresh your memory. So let me ask you this: Did you attend, were you present during the search of the persons who were taken out of the hospital on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this several times and I will repeat once again: Yes. I was present when these people were searched and taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, did you see that the persons searched entered the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Major Vukasinovic by the buses. Did you approach the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that yesterday or the day before, that I didn't approach the buses, but they were not far from me. I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long did the search take? I asked you that already, but would you please answer again.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The search, and this portion of the evacuation, took about two hours, give or take a minute. I'm not sure, given the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. There were some questions about the statement you gave to the OTP, where they inquired whether this was logical or that was logical. I will ask you about the 80th Brigade. Do you know that the military police company and that brigade secured the members of the so-called Mitnica group at Ovcara in the night between the 18th and 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I think, like you, I hadn't expected that that fact was of concern, but it appears to be of concern to Mr. Weiner so you were leading on it. I think you'd better be careful about leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't realise that there were problems concerning this. But I'll take this on board and I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, do you know, did you hear that at the command post or in any other place, it was discussed that there were problems concerning the guarding of the Mitnica battalion in the night between the 18th and 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that there were any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, when answering -- and also when answering questions put to you by the OTP, you said that in your view, it was logical for the securing to be done by the Guards Battalion, which had two military police units, that it be done by then rather than by one military police company. Let me ask you this: Do you know when the 80th Brigade was deployed to the Ovcara sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Brigade replaced a previous brigade at around the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the 80th Brigade took part in combat?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the military police company of the 80th Brigade was engaged in combat?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was, just like the brigade wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military police company was trained to carry out military police tasks?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is. All of them were reservists who had completed their military service in the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this: Is it logical then that the securing tasks be done by a unit, which is well-rested, which has full complement, which has not participated in combat operation, or do you think it's more logical for that task to be performed by a unit which saw combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, there is a further objection and it's well-founded. You are trying to argue your case through the witness. If you want him to tell you what he considered was most logical, you just ask him that and let him tell you. You're putting arguments as to why one was more logical than the other. If you could watch that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour, but that's precisely the type of questions that were put to Mr. Paunovic when the statement was taken from him. But all right, I will rephrase me question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Knowing all this, Mr. Paunovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I move to strike that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't strike, Mr. Weiner, as you might in your jurisprudence but no notice will be taken of it. There is absolutely no factual foundation for that assertion, Mr. Bulatovic. Not in the evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, in your view, who should be performing the security tasks related to persons? Should it be a unit whose area of responsibility it is, or should it be another unit outside of the area where the facility where the people are secured is located?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, it should be done by a unit whose area of responsibility it is. It shouldn't be done by an outside unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And can you repeat once again whose area of responsibility the sector of Ovcara was?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In answers given to the OTP, you said that when the evacuation was conducted at the Vukovar Hospital, you also saw some doctors. In your statement given to the OTP, you mentioned that, and I'd like to know how long did you talk with the representatives of the OTP during those two days, how many hours?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Belgrade, in the OTP office in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess that's where you met, unless you met some place else.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked for two days. Our interview would begin at 9.00 in the morning at conclude at 1900 hours. Naturally we had breaks, lunch breaks. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So two days. On that occasion, did you speak to them about the presence of doctors at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all of the details but perhaps there were some questions of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you enter the Vukovar Hospital during this evacuation that we are referring to now on the 20th, from the moment when you came to the hospital until this task described you; namely, the searching and taking of persons to the buses, was concluded?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for me entering the hospital, I entered only the first part of the hospital which is a corridor. And then from this corridor, if you go straight or to the right, you can enter several offices, doctors' offices or something like that. And further on the areas where the wounded were and the patients, those were the areas where I didn't enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The briefings you had on the 19th, the ones you described, and then you briefing on the 18th or any earlier one, was it ever mentioned that the persons who would be evacuated would be taken to Ovcara? Was Ovcara ever mentioned as a location?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, there were many questions concerning who was in charge in your view, in charge of evacuation. Do you know which rank was held by Mr. Sljivancanin during the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rank of Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which rank Mr. Pavkovic had during the Vukovar evacuation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Pavkovic an officer from a superior command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, where there are officers of different ranks, senior ones, junior ones, what would be your conclusion? Who could be in charge of that operation, of that mission?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would conclude that the officer with the senior rank from the superior command was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The taking away of Marin Vidic was discussed here on the 19th in the evening. You explained how you saw him, where you saw him, that you were reported -- or rather, you received information from the command. You said that it was even possible that you saw Sljivancanin before you went to the briefing in Negoslavci, or, rather, that he asked you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we put Exhibit 107 on the screen, page 11, please. This is the rules of service, Article 23. The previous page, please, page 11. Or rather, I apologise, 19. In English, it's page 11. Exhibit 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, these are the rules of service of security organs the armed forces of the Socialist Federalist Republic of Yugoslavia. Would you please read paragraph 3 of Article 23 which starts with the words: "The deployment of units," do you see that bit?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. "The deployment of units or individual members of the military police to perform tasks within the security organ's competence is determined by the security organ officer under paragraph 1 of this item with the approval of his superior military officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Paunovic, given your evidence that you were informed by the command that you needed to bring Marin Vidic, if such a request was put to you by Veselin Sljivancanin, in your view, would that be a legal request, given this rule on the cooperation between security organs and the military police?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be consistent with this article, paragraph 3, about the competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, I need just a few more seconds. I think I'm very close to being finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were told and you confirmed that within the 1st Battalion of the military police, there was an anti-terrorist company?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the strength it had an anti-terrorist company, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Paunovic, whether other units in the armed forces of the SFRY also had anti-terrorist companies or units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other units had some type of anti-terrorist units but not of this composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You answered a question put to you by the OTP saying that the organ -- security organ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I hear the term "advises" or "gives advice" in our vocabulary, we would say "proposes" or "gives specialist guidance" and so on. So that's the type of assistance he provides to the commander. We use that kind of vocabulary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Paunovic, you're quite right. That is precisely the vocabulary. Let me ask you this: Once the proposal is given for the military police units to be used, tell us, or rather, is that proposal given before the units are deployed or used?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, proposal is given before the units are deployed, and it is up to the commander whether he's going to accept such a proposal or not, proposal given by the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Once the military police unit is deployed or used, would you agree with me that there is no longer any point to give any proposals of how to use a unit because the unit has already been used?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. Once again, it's leading. There are other ways to ask it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite all right. Mr. Weiner is fully right. I was just trying to clear any ambiguities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Paunovic, let me ask you this: The 2nd Battalion of the military police, when it was deployed to secure the hospital, did it mean that it was used?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The decision -- or, rather, who issued you the order to carry out that task?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that that's the end of the evidence that you are asked to give here. The Chamber would like to thank you for your assistance and for coming here in this matter. So you are now free to leave and return to your other interests. You will be shown out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we wait for the next witness, Mr. Borovic, there's a matter concerning you. It has just been realised that the annex to your motion for the admission of documents was not filed under seal. It contains matters that enable the identification of three protected witnesses, which is a matter of considerable concern. The immediate need is for notice to be filed today with the Registry requesting that the annex be placed under seal. That is the effect of how it is being held at the moment under order of the Chamber, but we need an indication that it's under seal. And it is, I repeat, of considerable concern that the annex was filed openly concerning one or two witnesses, including one that you had sought to have the protective measures lifted. It's also interesting that the Prosecution response was filed under seal but made no mention of the absence of your own schedule as being not under seal. Now, this is a lapse that must not occur in future filings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just inform you on behalf of the Defence that it will be rectified in the course of the day. I apologise for this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness comes in, I have two issues to raise. One is that I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that we are not going to call one witness on our list, but I would prefer to give the reasons in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another issue, Your Honours. I can inform you that as the witness is brought in. It has to do with a request, since I cannot affect the length of cross-examination. And in Mr. Sljivancanin case, he was cross-examined a bit longer than the examination-in-chief; and the same applies to Mr. Paunovic. When we made our assessment, we were using one-third to two-thirds ratio and therefore, I would like to urge all parties to have that proportion in mind. So it isn't only our team that is mindful of the time, but also everybody else. I realise that everybody has questions to put, but I would still like to urge the parties to stick to the schedule provided so that we can be sure that we will stay within the limits. That's all I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not surprising, Mr. Lukic, that an accused might be cross-examined longer than an ordinary witness, not at all surprising, but my memory is that your examination of Mr. -- of the last witness, Mr. Paunovic, was longer than the cross-examination. I'm just checking my notes. It was the whole of the first day and Mr. Borovic didn't start until 10.00 on the second day. It was Mr. Domazet as well. So I think cross-examination may not have been the problem in either case. Very well. Good morning, sir. Sorry we were discussing another matter when you came in. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please tell us your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have already talked about the rhythm of question and answer we should maintain. So please bear in mind that you should pause between question and answer, and I will do the same although I have often been reminded to do so. I will now go through your career and CV very quickly. So please interrupt me if something I say is not correct. Your family situation is such that unfortunately, you have recently been widowed and you have two children. I would like to thank you for agreeing to come and testify in spite of your difficult family situation. And I do so on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's team, and I hope on the behalf of all the participants in these proceedings. Mr. Panic, you are a retired General; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you graduated from military academy. After that in the period from 1972 to 1984, you served in a garrison in inland Serbia, where you progressed from company commander to battalion commander and higher up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the Pozarevac garrison, and I progressed from platoon commander to company commander and further on, up to battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From 1984 to 1985, you went to the staff command school for tactical operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you joined the Guards Brigade in Belgrade with the rank of Major, and your first post there was as an officer in the operations and training department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1989, you were appointed Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, you had the rank of Colonel--

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- or rather junior Colonel, and then you were promoted to Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In mid-1992, you were appointed commander of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after the JNA was transformed into the army of Yugoslavia, from 1993 to 1996, you were corps commander of the special units of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From 1996 to 1999, you were assistant chief of the general staff of the army of Yugoslavia for the ground forces; and at the same time, you were the chief of the ground forces sector of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then, you graduated from the highest school of the Yugoslav army, the School of National Defence; and in 1995, you were promoted to rank of Major General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1999, you became the chief of the administration for housing. And from 2000 to 2002, chief of the inspection of combat readiness of the army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, due to the needs of the service, you retired in 1992 [As interpreted] with the rank of Lieutenant Colonel General?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I would also like to go quickly through the facts with regard to the Vukovar events about which you gave more than one statements. The sides in the proceedings know this, but for the sake of the Court, the first statement you made about the Vukovar events was made on the 20th of December, 1998 before the military court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you made the brief statement to the security organs within the brigade, and that was an additional part of the proceedings before the military court on the 9th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also interviewed or, rather, heard as a witness first by the investigating judge in Novi Sad in the proceedings that we commonly refer to as the Belgrade-Ovcara on the 28th of November, 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you testified in these proceedings on the 26th of November, 2004?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then, the OTP in The Hague interviewed you; and on the 25th to the 26th of July, 2005, last year, they interviewed you in their Belgrade office where you spoke to them for two days?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will leave these statements later on to the -- for the participants to look at. When did you first contact the team of Veselin Sljivancanin, his Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: In July of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you contact?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I contacted you, and the reason was for me to tell you what I remember, describe the events in Vukovar, and testify. And I agreed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did we have the most detailed conversations about all these events?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, we spoke most working together here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When considering your CV, we already said when you joined the Guards Brigade. But I would only like to know, as I would like to pass on as quickly as possible to the matter in hand, the persons who are sitting behind me, were they in the Guards Brigade, or do you know where they were when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Guards Brigade, all three were in the Guards Brigade. I'm not sure about Radic, whether he arrived after I did, but I have known Radic for quite a long time. As for Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin, they were in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Panic, I think that you are competent to testify about various matters, but, first of all, about the organisation and structure of the Guards Brigade. Can you tell us briefly what the main task of the Guards Brigade was, and how it differed from other motorised brigades of the then JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well very briefly, the Guards Brigade, as in all countries in the world, was an elite unit of the state and of the army. The Guards Brigade of the then Yugoslav national army was unique. It had its own special organisation and establishment, and specific tasks which differed from the everyday tasks of other brigades. The main task of the Guards Brigade was to secure high-ranking persons, VIPs, and special facilities. Furthermore, it conducted training and had duties related to the protocol. In line with this, the units were organised and the establishment set up. I can tell you what the brigade had in its composition that other brigades did not have. It had two motorised battalions. It had two battalions of the military police, and let me mention straight away that the military police battalions are something that no other brigade had. Other brigades had military police companies. Furthermore, there was a battalion for securing facilities and persons. This is also something that does not exist in other brigades. Also, the brigade had other units just like other brigades. There's no need to go into detail, but it did not have its own artillery, as other brigades do. If you need further details, I can go into that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at a document. This is a new document, Your Honours. It has been provided to all the participants in the proceedings. We received it only in September through the National Council. It is the Establishment Book of the Guards Brigade from 1991. It's 3D050286. And the English version is 3D050299. Could we please briefly look at the first page. I apologise, what I have just said is the B/C/S version, 3D050299. The English version is 0328. We have hard copies for the Chamber and for the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. They do not have these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could we please have this on the screen to give it to the Judges and the Prosecutor. [Interpretation] And a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the first page of this document. Was this the template that was in force in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 3, the diagram of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and could you explain what the difference was between the Guards Brigade and the other brigades in the then JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: This diagram resembles that of other Guards Brigades, but there are certain differences. As I said, only two motorised battalions. Other brigades had more, four to five motorised battalions. Then we have an armoured battalion, a military police, or rather two military police battalions. In other brigades, there was only a military police company. Then we have a battalion for providing security. This does not exist in other brigades. As I said, this brigade was unique.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, a point of clarification. Is this correct? The diagram we have only has one motorised battalion and one military police battalion. Is there something that's missing? Is there another page that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's pointed out to me, Mr. Weiner and Mr. Lukic, that underneath Motorised Battalion A and Military Police Battalion A, there is, on the next line on the right-hand side in each square, a number one. And that is not found on any other battalions. It may be the answer but clearly Mr. Lukic will explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, it's possible that the diagram in English does not correspond to the B/C/S we have on the screen. You have heard what the Prosecutor said. Does this diagram show there were two battalions of the military police and two motorised battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. It can clearly be seen here, and I know in fact that there were two motorised battalions and two military police battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Weiner has now seen this on the screen. You can see this in the B/C/S version. It's possible that in the English version, the square is not represented in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, can you continue?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, I left off speaking about the security battalion. It had up to 700 men, and its task was to provide security for buildings and military personnel. I wish to mention straight away that this battalion did not participate in the tasks of the Guards Brigade that we will be talking about. The next unit is the light artillery -- artillery battalion, and then there was the engineer's company, the communications company, and atomic, biological, and chemical company. That was something that was specific or peculiar to this brigade. Then there is the organ for moral guidance. It also had an orchestra, and this was also something that was unique to the Guards Brigade. Furthermore, in the command, there was an organ for special technology and communications. And there was also a platoon for special technology and communications, and it had to maintain communications between the top state leadership and the whole world. The security organ, as in other brigades, although it was stronger here, it also had a military police squad for special purposes. This does not exist in other units. These are persons who escort and provide security for high-ranking army and state officials. Then there was the organ for the rear, the organ for planning and the financial affairs, and rear battalion as in other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This special-purpose squad which we see is directly linked to the security organ, do you know whether this squad participated in the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, it did not. They were carrying out their usual tasks, because the state leadership was active at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To avoid leading, were they securing Mr. Kadijevic, Mr. Adzic, and people such as they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, both the state and army top leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, who made up the command of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The command of the Guards Brigade comprised the staff. Organ for moral guidance, organ for special technology and communications, security organ, a logistics organ or rear organ, and organ for planning and material and financial transactions. Naturally, they have their own organs and their communication links in the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about battalion commanders? Who were they subordinated to from whom they received their orders and to whom they reported?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Battalion commanders were directly subordinated to the brigade commander, and you can see this in this organigramme.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will put another question to you about this document. At the brigade staff, was there something else that was peculiar? Were there any other persons who were not part of some other staffs within the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: We already said that both the command and the unit were of a unique composition, given the role and the task of the Guards Brigade. I was the Chief of Staff. Within the staff, there existed all other organs as in other brigades. But there was a unique feature here where we had an officer within the operations and training organ who was in charge of proposing, and he was simply in charge of the combat readiness. And he gave proposals for training; he had an overview of the combat readiness and level of training of the military police. So to put it briefly, there was an officer for military police battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which normally does not exist within other staffs; there are no representatives of military police within other staffs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I was Chief of Staff, and I can give you exactly, precisely the names of the organs, which were part of the staff, including this particular officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this document be admitted into evidence. There are some other issues that can be covered, but I think we'll leave that for experts. In the meantime, could we have this document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Noting that there are some amendments necessary to the English language version of the chart. Are you tendering the whole of the document or just that? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 851, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, before the break, perhaps we can cover another topic. What was the task -- or rather, what mission was the Guards Brigade given when it was sent to Vukovar? When did it go to Vukovar, the Guards Brigade? It was in late September, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was deployed on a mission on the 30th of September, 1991. Its mission was to deblock the barracks in Vukovar where soldiers and officers alike had been under siege for a long time. It was probably mentioned here that they did not have food, water, medical assistance. They couldn't even bury their dead, because they were constantly under siege, under blockade, and subject to cross-fire of snipers. Very often, mortar shells and other kinds of ammunition were used to target the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the barracks was deblocked, and what was the other reason of the deployment of the brigade to the area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Prior to us, another unit attempted to accomplish this mission. It was a unit from Sremska Mitrovica. On the 2nd of October, we passed through their combat disposition; and on the 2nd of October, the barracks was liberated. We were united with our soldiers and officers in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that the barracks was deblocked on that date. You contacted your unit - and I'm just correcting the transcript - on page 32 line 3, you said that the barracks was deblocked; there is a mistake in the transcript. Why did the brigade remain in Vukovar? We know very well that it remained there until the 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I could give you a long story about the deployment of the brigade and the time it spent in the area, but more or less, it is all well-known. Simply, the conclusion was that after the siege of the barracks was lifted, we found ourselves under a semi-siege. We were semi-encircled. Before coming to this area, we expected that our mission would be easy. That, simply speaking, owing to minor preparations, basically on the move, we would be able to resolve the problems which were the reason we had been sent to Vukovar in the first place. On the 2nd of October, we were stopped by very strong resistance of the paramilitary formations; and when we found ourselves semi-encircled, we halted our offensive. We had losses among our troops and also in weaponry, and it was necessary for us to regroup our forces and to prepare for a different type of combat. In addition, we issued a call to paramilitary formations to put down their weapons and to thus bring our mission to the end. They did not accept that, the combat continued in the following days, but a different tactics was applied in the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to another topic. Your Honours, I think this would be a good time for our first break today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We will have the first break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Panic, we have, as an agreed fact, that the Guards Brigade became incorporated into the Operations Group South. My question is: Was there a change within the command and in the role of the commander of the Operations Group South, what happened, and who became the commander, and who comprised the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was deployed on its mission pursuant to the order of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, and the brigade was resubordinated to the 1st Military District. Within that, it became part of the Operations Group South. The Operations Group South had already been in the area where we came, and the Guards Brigade just became part of it. This situation continued until the 8th of October - I think, but you can verify in the documents - at which time, Colonel Mile Mrksic, commander of the Guards Brigade became commander of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there the command of the Operations Group South; and if so, who did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The rules and regulations provide that the command of the Operations Group South had a powerful composition. Based on the principles, it should be command of the corps or division. However, in our situation, the command of OG South consisted of the command of the Guards Brigade. Typically, there were two colonels from the superior command there who, pursuant to the order of the chief of cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, were sent one of the command of the brigade and the other one to the artillery organ of the brigade. These two colonels were Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic, and Zlatoje Terzic, whose specialty was artillery. These are the only reinforcements in our command, including the command of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will discuss the meetings later on and who attended the meetings of the OG South. Do you remember whether there was a written document? Do you remember seeing a written document, pursuant to which the Guards Brigade became command of OG South? We saw an entry in the war diary about the commander. But do you remember whether there was a written order, and who was it supposed to be issued by if there was one?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: There was an order, and it was only pursuant to that order that we could have taken over this role. And it was allegedly an order issued by the command of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask you something about the daily meetings at the command. When were they held? Maybe I was leading when I said "daily." But at what time, and who took activity participation in the meetings, in drafting decisions, and making them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The meetings were held almost daily. There were some exceptions when, due to combat or some activities that had been commenced, a daily briefing would not be held. However, on those occasions, tasks would be issued on the move. That is to say, during the execution of previously-issued tasks, meetings would normally be held towards the evening, beginning typically at 1800 hours. Commander of the brigade would typically chair the meeting, Colonel Mrksic. The meeting was attended by subordinate commanders, his assistants and myself, as chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by this, subordinate commanders? Can you remember who were these people? Can you give us their positions and their names, and we are mostly interested in the final period, the second half of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Subordinate commanders were battalion commanders and commanders of Assault Detachments. Commander of the 1st Battalion, and at one point in time, commander of the Assault Detachment, Borivoje Tesic; commander of the 2nd was Adem Bajic and later Branislav Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please go slower with the names for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Commander of the 1st Battalion of military police was initially Kavalic Branislav. Later on, this role was taken over by Jovan Susic. Commander of the 2nd Battalion of military police was Blagoje Paunovic. Commander of armoured battalion was Tomic. Commanders of brigades, first of all the 20th Brigade, was Misovic Slobodan, and then the 80th Motorised Brigade, Vojnovic. Commander of the local TO was Jaksic. During one period of time, there was also Milo Miladinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his role?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: He had a special unit, special detachment which comprised of volunteer units in the central part of Vukovar. He was either a Major or Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA. The rest were assistants of the commander and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The assistants you described, when looking at the organigramme?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. If it is relevant, I omitted one detachment, the 3rd Assault Detachment. It was commanded by Milorad Stupar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I don't want to be leading but his unit was not from the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No. There were many units there that were not in the main establishment of the Guards Brigade, the original establishment. They were there simply for the purpose of performing a certain task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So all the commanders in our Operative Group South were present at the meetings of commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, put quite simply, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did a meeting proceed? What would a regular meeting look like?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: A meeting would begin with the commander opening the meeting. He would provide an overview of the situation for the past day. He would hear the brief reports given by his subordinate commanders. He would hear reports and suggestions of his assistants, and issue orders containing the tasks for the following day. Sometimes these would even be long-term tasks for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With respect to daily activities and these meetings -- well, first of all, were minutes made at these regular meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. The most important information was entered into the war diary. Initially, there was also an operations diary that was kept. But, as I mentioned, the brigade command also took on the role of commanding Operations Group South, where some of the officers in the command, and primarily from the staff, had to be engaged in carrying out daily tasks in the units. After a while, no operations diary were kept, but, rather, the most important information was entered into the war diary and some in the registry book. Thus, the gap was filled that was created because no operative log was kept, orders issued and received and information coming to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the course of your time in Vukovar, from whom did you receive orders, to whom did you send reports? I'm referring to the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The Operations Group South received its tasks either in written or in oral form from the command of the 1st Military District. It also sent reports to the 1st Military District. Of course, there were some reports that were not sent to the 1st Military District, but to the office of the Secretary for National Defence. These were the reports sent by the security organ, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question concerning these meetings. The local TO commander Dusan Jaksic was present. We heard in testimony before this Tribunal that at one point, he was replaced and that Miroljub Vujovic was appointed in his place. My first question is: Have you heard of this person, and did he attend any of the meetings of the commands of the Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Jaksic, as the commander of the local Territorial Defence, did attend these meetings. And at one point before the end of the fighting in Vukovar, Miroljub Vujovic was appointed to Jaksic's position. He did not attend the meetings. The reason was that the units were regrouped, and he was put under the command of Major Tesic in the left wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Into the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave us some details about the keeping of the war diary, so we will look at two entries now. But before that, let me ask you the following: Were the borders of the area of responsibility of Operations Group South delineated, and were areas of responsibility within it defined?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. An order was issued and explained orally on the ground. The right-hand border was the River Danube, the left-hand border was the Vuka River, the axis of attack, the area of Negoslavci and the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within the operations group itself --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, within the Operations Group South, areas of responsibility were divided up. This is always done, even when maneuvers are carried out. Each Assault Detachment and each battalion had its own borders and could carry out its tasks within those borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now briefly look at the entry in the war diary, Exhibit 401, English version page 19, B/C/S version page 20. This is the entry of the 9th of October, 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you will see it on the screen, and I will read it out. After that, I will ask you to comment on it. The entry for the 9th of October at 0800 hours reads as follows: "The commander of the 1st Military District arrived in the command of Operations Group South and gave the task for the Operations Group South to maintain the belt from the River Vuka to the Danube. He established the precise zone of area of responsibility and gave information about the other units of the 1st Military District. He had information about the situation," and there follows an illegible word, "in the areas." He set out the information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He set out the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, first of all, who arrived where you were, and do you remember these facts entered here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, the fact that the commander of the 1st Military District visited our command more than once, and this is one of his visits. His other visits, if you look at the war diary, are also entered into the war diary. And there is always a brief description of the occasion of his visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As this entry is dated the 9th of October, did the commander of the 1st District, when he defined the area of responsibility, during the combat operations, did he change this area from the River Vuka to the River Danube?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No. The left-hand border was kept until the end, except when, after the liberation of Vukovar, the order was issued that Operations Group South should also liberate the hospital and carry out the procedures we will be probably talking about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us when the Operations Group was given the task of crossing the River Vuka?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at just one more entry from this document. But before that, I will put another question to you because it's on a different topic. Mr. Panic, during the combat operations, did you go to the front lines to tour the troops?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did, very often, in all units. I spent more time with the units on the right wing where there were more problems. As regards carrying out the designated task, I spent less time in the left wing where discipline was better and there was more success.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was on the left wing, and who was on the right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: When I say the left wing, I'm referring to the 1st Assault Detachment. When I say the right wing, this includes the units in direction of the barracks and around the barracks, the units at Mitnica, and the units at Vucedol, all the way up to the Danube River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you say that you often went into the field, so to say, can you tell us what you mean by "often", once a fortnight or every day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was almost every day. The reason for this was, first of all, to precisely define the tasks on the ground. This is best done in personal contact with the soldiers and their officers, their commanders. I'm not trying to glorify my own role. This was done by all commanders, but I am now talking about what I did. So I visited the men and their commanders on the front line. There was also the issue of morale in certain units because, in one period of time, morale did not meet our requirements, primarily in some units that had been mobilised and some volunteer units. And of course on my return, I would know firsthand what their problems were, what their needs were, and also I would be aware of how true their evening reports were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At these briefings or while you were in the command or in the field, did you learn whether Major Sljivancanin was also frequently visiting the front lines, and did you know if he did visit the front lines, why he did so?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin also visited the units daily. Major Sljivancanin, in addition to the task of surveying the situation in the field, had other security problems which he resolved on the spot; a huge area of responsibility, many problems arising, especially when we started liberating the town quarter by quarter, and when people started emerging. And one had to see from the security point of view, whether these were fighters or just civilians and what should be done with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at the entry in this same exhibit dated the 4th of October, at 10.40, this is page 6 both in the B/C/S and the English version. I will read it. It's the time entered is 10.40. "1: Huge concentration of Ustasha in the Dunav Hotel; 2: In the worker's congress hall, 3: In the municipality, 4: In Olajnice at the bus station, 5: A sniper captured, Vlatko Bajen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Can provide information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the notes, it says, "information received from Colonel Pavkovic." My question is: Do you remember that Colonel Pavkovic also frequently toured the units, and that he also personally provided such information at meetings of the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Pavkovic was extremely useful to us at the command post. He frequently visited the units. And towards the end of the combat operations, he had intensive talks with international organisations and representatives of the Red Cross. He did a lot to deal with persons appearing in the town of Vukovar after its liberation; that is, organising transport and participating in their screening and the separation of the combatants from the non-combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The seat of the security organ - I will use my client's term - of the Guards Brigade, was it in the same building of the command of Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No. I can tell you what organs were in the same building as Operations Group South, but he was in house number nine, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, in view of your position and your tasks, did you know anything about the way information was passed between the security organ, specifically Sljivancanin and whoever else? Who did he report to, and who communicated with him; both within the Operations Group and outside it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Well, Major Sljivancanin was the chief of the security organ and also the assistant commander for security. In his work, he had a team of men in carrying out his work, that is. These were also men from the security organ. There is a list of their names - I don't want to dwell on it now - and together with them, he gained insights into the security situation in the area of responsibility. What was important to the commander was something that he briefed the commander on. He was also duty-bound to report up his chain of command in the security organ in his specialty. So he had to report, at that time, it was Djukic who was in charge of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Blagoje Adzic came. Were you present when the chief of the General Staff visited?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I saw him only briefly. I was not part of the delegation who met him and who escorted him. He wanted to tour some units and he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, during your stay in Vukovar, Vojislav Seselj came there? Did you personally see him? Do you know anything about his visits, if any?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Vojislav Seselj came once, to my knowledge. And I know that he visited the units within the 1st Assault Detachment, that is to say, specifically, the unit called Leva Supoderica whose commander was called Kameni Lancuzanin. I was not present -- I wasn't in his company; and as far as I know, he didn't stay long in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. If you had no direct contact with him --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And I could only tell you about what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the artillery of OG South fire outside of its area of responsibility during combat operations? Was it active outside of its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The artillery, in its mission, receives very detailed information about the area where they are to fire; and, based on that, they plan their fire. They were not supposed to fire at targets outside of their area or, rather, outside of the approved plan. If something of that sort happened, a commission was established instantly to investigate the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During combat operations, did you receive information that the artillery of OG South fired upon the hospital at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Our artillery, that of OG South, never fired on the hospital and the sector around the hospital; and I can emphasise here that this was particularly highlighted during regular briefings. Nobody could fire at such targets. If I can support this with a fact: Starting on the 2nd of October, there were already our soldiers in the hospital, that is to say, we had an officer and several soldiers there. Jovic was a sergeant, and then there was several soldiers. Jovic left the hospital on the 19th. He was wounded but he survived; and throughout that time, he was at the hospital. That was one more reason for commanders to abstain from firing at any targets across from the Vuka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of more technical questions, because I believe that you are competent to answer them. If there is an evacuation of the wounded or an evacuation of the prisoners, or conduct of prisoners, operations of that sort need to involve what kind of persons in order for such a mission to be carried out properly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: This is a very serious and responsible task, and relevant command organs need to be involved in such a task, including specialty organs which carry out the task. First of all, this involves security tasks, then it involves tasks from the area of medical corps and logistics. These tasks must be planned individually and specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If a task is outside of the regular scope of competence of an officer, how can such a task be issued?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: It can be issued both verbally and in writing. If the task has or carries material or any other sort of responsibility, then it needs to be in writing, in order to protect such an officer, if such a task goes beyond his area of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we briefed you for your evidence, you said that you were not familiar in detail with the rules on the work of security organs. In your view, can a security organ be issued tasks that fall outside of its competence as prescribed by the rules of service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Commander can issue an order to any subordinate officer. An officer is duty-bound to carry it out, except if such a task entails criminal responsibility. It is not typical that a security organ is issued with a task that normally falls within the scope of competence of another organ, specialty organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a detailed or written order on evacuation specifying who is to do what? I'm referring to the evacuation carried out on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: The tasks were assigned verbally in relation to that evacuation. I do not remember that -- or at least we cannot find a single written document where such tasks were given in detail, specifying role position, type of task, and so on. It was all done verbally, except that we received a written order from the command of the 1st Military District. That was the basis on which we proceeded in order to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, did you personally take part in negotiations and surrender of the Mitnica group, which was actually Mitnica detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: I know exactly when that group surrendered. That was a unit numbering 170 people. That was on the 18th of November. But I wasn't present in the area on that day, nor did I have any kind of a task related to that unit or its surrender. If necessary, I can tell you where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was in the sector of the water tower. We hoisted Yugoslav flag on the water tower, because the main combat in Vukovar ceased on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, or perhaps did you watch any footage, or did you hear about the Mitnica surrender, and as to whether weapons were surrendered as well on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. We know that -- we know, on the basis of the contact with people who took part in implementing that task, and it is generally well-known that these people asked for surrender. This was widely known. We called for surrender from day one. The people from Mitnica, who put up fierce resistance, asked for surrender. The surrender was accepted.
